---
title: "P1 exercises — Building a functioning plant"
---

The questions follow the [tutorial](index.qmd) and [slides](lec.qmd). Answer
each question before opening its answer.

## Cell compartments

### 1.1

Match each structure to its main function.

| | Structure |
| --- | --- |
| A | Plasma membrane |
| B | Primary cell wall |
| C | Tonoplast |
| D | Chloroplast |
| E | Mitochondrion |

Functions: (1) membrane surrounding the central vacuole; (2) site of
photosynthesis; (3) selective control of exchange between the cytoplasm and
the outside of the cell; (4) site of aerobic respiration; (5) resists
deformation and constrains the direction of expansion.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

A–3, B–5, C–1, D–2, E–4.
:::

### 1.2

Define *turgor pressure* and state what happens to a non-woody shoot when
turgor falls.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Turgor pressure is the positive hydrostatic pressure of the cell contents
against the cell wall, produced when water enters a cell with a resisting wall.
When turgor falls, the cells lose rigidity and the shoot wilts, even though the
cells may still be alive.
:::

### 1.3

Name three functions of the large central vacuole of a mature plant cell.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Any three of: storage of solutes (ions, sugars, organic acids, pigments,
defensive compounds); generation of turgor by solute accumulation and water
uptake; regulation of cytoplasmic pH; degradation of cellular material;
allowing the cell to enlarge without making a corresponding volume of
cytoplasm.
:::

### 1.4

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. All plastids are chloroplasts.
b. Leaf cells respire only in darkness.
c. The cell wall is selectively permeable and controls which solutes enter the cell.
d. Many root cells lack photosynthetically active chloroplasts.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. False. Chloroplasts are one type of plastid; others include amyloplasts
   (starch storage) and chromoplasts (pigments).
b. False. Mitochondrial respiration continues in light and darkness.
c. False. Water and small solutes pass through the wall; selective control is
   exercised by the plasma membrane.
d. True.
:::

## Cell walls, growth and cell connections

### 2.1

Name the main load-bearing component of the primary cell wall and the polymer
that reinforces secondary walls of xylem conduits.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Cellulose microfibrils (embedded in a matrix of hemicelluloses, pectins and
proteins). Secondary walls of xylem conduits are reinforced by lignin.
:::

### 2.2

Turgor pressure is present, but a cell does not enlarge irreversibly. Name the
wall property that must change to allow growth, and the two materials that
must be supplied as the cell enlarges.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

The wall must be loosened so that it yields (extends irreversibly) under
turgor. New wall material and new plasma membrane must be supplied.
:::

### 2.3

Define *apoplast*, *symplast* and *plasmodesma*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

- **Apoplast:** the continuous system of cell walls and extracellular spaces
  outside the plasma membranes (including the lumens of dead xylem conduits).
- **Symplast:** the cytoplasm of cells connected through plasmodesmata.
- **Plasmodesma:** a membrane-lined channel through the cell wall that connects
  the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells.
:::

### 2.4

A solute moves from the apoplast into the symplast. Which structure must it
cross?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

The plasma membrane of a cell.
:::

## Tissues and organs

### 3.1

Complete the table for the three tissue systems.

| Tissue system | Main functions | One example of a cell or tissue type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dermal | | |
| Ground | | |
| Vascular | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Tissue system | Main functions | One example of a cell or tissue type |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dermal | Protection; control of exchange with the environment | Epidermis, guard cells, root hairs |
| Ground | Photosynthesis, storage, support | Mesophyll (parenchyma), collenchyma, sclerenchyma |
| Vascular | Long-distance transport; support | Xylem, phloem |
:::

### 3.2

Complete the table for the three ground-tissue cell types.

| | Parenchyma | Collenchyma | Sclerenchyma |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Living at maturity? | | | |
| Wall | | | |
| Main function | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Parenchyma | Collenchyma | Sclerenchyma |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Living at maturity? | Yes | Yes | Usually no |
| Wall | Thin primary wall | Unevenly thickened primary wall | Thick, lignified secondary wall |
| Main function | Metabolism, photosynthesis, storage | Flexible support of growing organs | Rigid support (fibres, sclereids) |
:::

### 3.3

Name the cell or tissue that matches each description.

| | Description |
| --- | --- |
| A | Elongated conducting cell, dead at maturity, with thick lignified walls and perforated end walls |
| B | Living conducting cell without a nucleus, joined end to end through sieve plates |
| C | Living cell with a nucleus that lies beside B and supports its function |
| D | Pair of cells that border a pore in the leaf epidermis |
| E | Tubular extension of a root epidermal cell |
| F | Cell layer around the root vascular cylinder carrying the Casparian strip |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

A: vessel element (xylem). B: sieve-tube element (phloem). C: companion cell.
D: guard cells. E: root hair. F: endodermis.
:::

### 3.4

Complete the table comparing xylem and phloem.

| | Xylem | Phloem |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main substances transported | | |
| Conducting cells | | |
| Conducting cells living at maturity? | | |
| Direction of transport | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Xylem | Phloem |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main substances transported | Water and mineral ions | Sugars (mainly sucrose), amino acids, signals |
| Conducting cells | Tracheids and vessel elements | Sieve-tube elements (with companion cells) |
| Conducting cells living at maturity? | No | Yes, but without a nucleus |
| Direction of transport | Roots to shoot | From sources to sinks, up or down |

Xylem as a tissue still contains living parenchyma cells; only the conducting
cells are dead.
:::

### 3.5

Give the order in which CO₂ passes these leaf structures on its way from the
atmosphere to the site of fixation: mesophyll cell, stomatal pore, chloroplast
stroma, intercellular air space, plasma membrane.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Stomatal pore → intercellular air space → plasma membrane → mesophyll cell
(cytosol) → chloroplast stroma. CO₂ dissolves in the water of the wet cell
wall before crossing the plasma membrane.
:::

### 3.6

Why does opening the stomata increase both CO₂ uptake and water loss?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

CO₂ diffuses in and water vapour diffuses out through the same pore. The
cuticle is nearly impermeable to both, so opening the pore raises the
conductance for both gases at once.
:::

## Meristems and growth

### 4.1

Name the meristem responsible for each of the following.

a. Increase in length of a root
b. Production of secondary xylem and secondary phloem
c. Production of the protective outer bark tissue (periderm)
d. Regrowth of a grass leaf after its tip has been cut

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Root apical meristem. b. Vascular cambium (secondary xylem inward,
secondary phloem outward). c. Cork cambium (phellogen). d. Intercalary
(basal) meristem.
:::

### 4.2

A root segment contains 100 cells arranged end to end. Ignore spaces between
cells.

a. Calculate the segment length in mm when the mean cell length is 40 µm.
b. With no cell division, the mean cell length becomes 70 µm. Calculate the new
   segment length and the increase.
c. How many 40 µm cells would give the same final length as in (b)?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 100 × 40 µm = 4000 µm = 4 mm.
b. 100 × 70 µm = 7000 µm = 7 mm; increase = 3 mm.
c. 7000 µm / 40 µm = 175 cells. The same length can result from cell
   expansion or from cell division, so length alone does not identify the
   process.
:::

### 4.3

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. Cell differentiation requires a change in the DNA sequence.
b. Primary growth increases the length of roots and shoots.
c. Every mature plant cell can regenerate a whole plant under any conditions.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. False. Differentiation results from differences in gene expression; the
   DNA sequence is unchanged.
b. True.
c. False. Some cells can resume division and regenerate, but this depends on
   genotype, developmental state and culture conditions.
:::

## Three genomes

### 5.1

Name the three genomes of a plant cell and state which one encodes most of
the proteins that function inside chloroplasts.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Nuclear, plastid (chloroplast) and mitochondrial genomes. Most chloroplast
proteins are encoded in the nucleus, synthesised in the cytosol and imported
into the chloroplast.
:::

### 5.2

A mutation in a nuclear gene encoding a chloroplast-imported protein reduces
photosynthesis, while the chloroplast DNA is unchanged. Is this possible?
Explain in one sentence.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Yes. The protein functions in the chloroplast but its gene is in the nucleus,
so a nuclear mutation can impair chloroplast function.
:::

### 5.3

Leaf and root cells of one plant have the same nuclear genome but different
functions. What is the reason?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

They express different sets of genes (tissue-specific gene expression).
:::

## Explore: Growth of a walled cell {#explore-p1-cellgrowth}

The demo models one elongating cell with the Lockhart equation, relative growth
rate r = φ(P − Y), where P is turgor, Y the wall yield threshold (both in MPa)
and φ the wall extensibility (MPa⁻¹ h⁻¹). Set the sliders or click a preset;
the readout gives r and the doubling time, and "Grow for 8 h" grows the cell
from 20 µm.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="p1-cellgrowth"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/p1-cellgrowth.js"></script>
```

### E1.1

Use the default settings (P = 0.60, Y = 0.30, φ = 1.0). What is the growth
rate r, the doubling time, and the cell length after 8 h (to the nearest µm)?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

r = 1.0 × (0.60 − 0.30) = 0.30 h⁻¹; doubling time ln 2 / 0.30 = 2.3 h;
length after 8 h = 20 × e^(0.30 × 8) ≈ 220 µm.
:::

### E1.2

Click "Stiff wall: P < Y" (P = 0.60, Y = 0.70). The cell is fully turgid. What
is the growth rate, and why?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

r = 0. Turgor (0.60 MPa) does not exceed the yield threshold (0.70 MPa), so
the wall only stretches elastically and does not yield. A turgid cell is not
necessarily a growing cell.
:::

### E1.3

Keep Y = 0.30. Which change gives the larger growth rate: (a) doubling φ to
2.0 with P = 0.60, or (b) raising P to 0.90 with φ = 1.0?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Neither: both give r = 0.60 h⁻¹ (2.0 × 0.30 and 1.0 × 0.60), with a doubling
time of 1.2 h. Doubling the extensibility has the same effect as doubling the
excess of turgor over the yield threshold.
:::

### E1.4

Click "Acid growth (auxin)" (P = 0.60, Y = 0.20, φ = 1.5). What is r, and by
what factor is it higher than in the default? Which wall proteins, activated
by low wall pH, does this preset represent?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

r = 1.5 × (0.60 − 0.20) = 0.60 h⁻¹, twice the default 0.30 h⁻¹. Turgor is
unchanged; the wall was loosened. Auxin stimulates plasma-membrane H⁺-ATPases,
the wall acidifies and expansins loosen the cellulose–hemicellulose network
(higher φ, lower Y).
:::

### E1.5

Click "Low turgor" (P = 0.35, Y = 0.30, φ = 1.0), as in a mildly
water-stressed root. What is r and the doubling time? Roughly how long is the
cell after 8 h?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

r = 1.0 × 0.05 = 0.05 h⁻¹, doubling time 13.9 h; after 8 h the cell is only
about 30 µm (20 × e^0.4 ≈ 29.8 µm). A small drop in turgor nearly stops growth
because only the excess above Y drives expansion.
:::

## Explore: Root growth, more cells or longer cells? {#explore-p1-roottip}

Two root tips, A and B, are shown with the tip held still on the right. Each
meristem produces new cells at a set rate per cell file; each cell leaves the
meristem at 10 µm, elongates to a set final length and then matures. Set the
two sliders for each root and press "Grow for 8 h"; the readouts give the
number of new cells, the distance the tip moved, and the growth rate.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../../demos/dist/demo.css">
<div data-demo="p1-roottip"></div>
<script src="../../demos/dist/p1-roottip.js"></script>
```

### E2.1

Use the "Slide example" (A: 2.2 cells/h, final length 40 µm; B: 1.25 cells/h,
70 µm) and grow for 8 h. How many new cells does each root make, and how far
does each tip move?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

A: 17 new cells, B: 10 new cells. Both tips move 0.70 mm (growth rates
2.2 × 40 = 88 µm/h and 1.25 × 70 = 87.5 µm/h). Root length alone cannot tell
the two roots apart.
:::

### E2.2

A drug that blocks cell division halves root A's cell production to 1.1
cells/h without changing the final cell length (40 µm). What is A's growth
rate, and how far does its tip move in 8 h?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

1.1 × 40 = 44 µm/h (0.044 mm/h); the tip moves 0.35 mm in 8 h, half as far
as before.
:::

### E2.3

Set root B's cell production to 1.10 cells/h. Which final cell length (slider
in steps of 5 µm) makes B grow at exactly the same rate as the default root A?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

80 µm: 1.1 × 80 = 88 µm/h = 2.2 × 40. Both tips then move 0.70 mm in 8 h.
:::

### E2.4

Click "Identical roots" (1.5 cells/h, 60 µm). Then set A's final cell length
to 120 µm, as in a mutant with more extensible walls. By what factor does A's
growth rate change, and which zone of the root tip is responsible?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

It doubles (from 1.5 × 60 = 90 µm/h to 1.5 × 120 = 180 µm/h). The change is
in the elongation zone, where cells expand; the meristem still produces the
same number of cells.
:::

## Bioinformatics and R {#bioinformatics}

Rubisco, the enzyme that fixes CO₂, is built from two kinds of subunit encoded
in two different genomes: the large subunit in the chloroplast and the small
subunit in the nucleus. A nuclear gene is not simply a string of codons: it has
exons and introns, untranslated regions (UTRs) and, for a chloroplast protein,
a stretch that codes for an address label. These exercises teach you to look up
plant genes by their **AGI code** in **TAIR**, **NCBI Gene** and **Ensembl
Plants**, to read a **gene structure**, and to use **R** to fetch the genomic
DNA, the mRNA, the coding sequence (CDS) and the protein of real genes and
compare them.

::: {.callout-tip}
## How to search for an Arabidopsis gene

**AGI codes.** Every *Arabidopsis thaliana* gene has an Arabidopsis Genome
Initiative code such as **AT1G67090**: `AT` = *A. thaliana*, `1` = chromosome
1 (`C` = chloroplast, `M` = mitochondrion), `G` = gene, `67090` = its number,
counting along the chromosome from the top in steps of 10. A suffix `.1`,
`.2` (AT1G67090.1) names a transcript (gene model) of that gene. AGI codes are
the safest search term, because gene names have synonyms.

**Where to search.**

- **TAIR** (<https://www.arabidopsis.org>): the Arabidopsis database. Search by
  AGI code or gene name; the locus page lists aliases, gene models and
  descriptions.
- **NCBI Gene** (<https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene>): query
  `RBCS1A[sym] AND "Arabidopsis thaliana"[orgn]` or simply the AGI code. The
  record shows the AGI code under "Also known as", the chromosome, the exon
  count and RefSeq sequences (NM_ = mRNA, NP_ = protein; NC_ = whole
  chromosome).
- **Ensembl Plants** (<https://plants.ensembl.org>, now part of
  <https://www.ensembl.org>): search the AGI code and open the gene. The gene
  page shows location, strand and each transcript drawn as boxes (exons) joined
  by lines (introns); coding parts are drawn as filled boxes, UTRs as open or
  thinner boxes.

**Four sequences of one gene.** *Genomic* DNA = exons + introns. *mRNA* (cDNA)
= exons only: 5′ UTR + CDS + 3′ UTR. *CDS* = from the ATG start codon to and
including the stop codon. *Protein* = CDS translated, so
CDS length = 3 × (protein length + 1).
:::

### B1. Finding the Rubisco small-subunit gene

a. Search NCBI Gene for `RBCS1A[sym] AND "Arabidopsis thaliana"[orgn]`. What is
   the AGI code of RBCS1A, and what does it tell you about the chromosome?
b. What is the NCBI Gene ID, and how many exons does the gene have?
c. Search Ensembl Plants (or TAIR) for the AGI code. Is the gene on the forward
   or the reverse strand?
d. Its curated RefSeq mRNA is **NM_105379.4**. Find it on the NCBI Gene page.
   What does the "4" after the dot mean? (A) the 4th transcript of the gene;
   (B) the 4th version of that sequence record.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. **AT1G67090**: an Arabidopsis gene on chromosome **1**, near the lower end
   (gene numbers on chromosome 1 run up to about 80000).
b. Gene ID **843029**; **3** exons.
c. **Reverse** strand (chromosome 1, about 25.05 Mb). The genomic sequence must
   therefore be read from the opposite strand to get the gene in its
   5′→3′ direction (B2 does this with `strand=2`).
d. **B.** The version number goes up whenever the sequence of the record is
   changed. Quoting accession *and* version (NM_105379.4) pins the exact
   sequence, so results can be repeated.
:::

### B2. One gene, four sequences

The code fetches, for RBCS1A, the genomic region from chromosome 1
(NC_003070.9, reverse strand), the mRNA and its CDS (NM_105379.4) from NCBI,
and the protein from UniProt (P10795).

```r
efetch <- "https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=nuccore&"
read_fasta <- function(url) paste(readLines(url)[-1], collapse = "")

genomic <- read_fasta(paste0(efetch,
  "id=NC_003070.9&seq_start=25048158&seq_stop=25049667&strand=2&rettype=fasta"))
mrna    <- read_fasta(paste0(efetch, "id=NM_105379.4&rettype=fasta"))
cds     <- read_fasta(paste0(efetch, "id=NM_105379.4&rettype=fasta_cds_na"))
protein <- read_fasta("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P10795.fasta")

c(genomic = nchar(genomic), mRNA = nchar(mrna),
  CDS = nchar(cds), protein = nchar(protein))
nchar(genomic) - nchar(mrna)          # removed by splicing
nchar(cds) / 3                        # codons in the CDS
substr(cds, nchar(cds) - 2, nchar(cds))   # last codon
as.integer(regexpr(cds, mrna))        # where the CDS starts in the mRNA
```

a. What are the lengths of the four sequences?
b. How many nucleotides are removed by splicing (total intron length)?
c. The CDS has 181 codons but the protein has 180 amino acids. Why, and which
   codon is the last one?
d. At which nucleotide of the mRNA does the CDS start? How long are the 5′ UTR
   and the 3′ UTR?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
genomic    mRNA     CDS protein
   1510    1268     543     180
[1] 242
[1] 181
[1] "TAA"
[1] 419
```

a. Genomic **1510** nt, mRNA **1268** nt, CDS **543** nt, protein **180** aa.
b. **242** nt of intron.
c. The last codon is the stop codon **TAA**, which is read by a release factor,
   not a tRNA, so it adds no amino acid: 543 = 3 × (180 + 1).
d. At nucleotide **419**, so the 5′ UTR is **418** nt; the 3′ UTR is
   1268 − 418 − 543 = **307** nt. Only 43 % of the mRNA is coding; the UTRs
   carry signals for translation and mRNA stability.
:::

### B3. Where are the introns, and what does exon 1 encode?

The Ensembl/NCBI gene page of transcript AT1G67090.1 gives the exon lengths
589, 135 and 544 nt, separated by introns of 106 and 136 nt. The code cuts the
genomic sequence into exons and introns, checks the intron ends and glues the
exons together.

```r
efetch <- "https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=nuccore&"
read_fasta <- function(url) paste(readLines(url)[-1], collapse = "")
genomic <- read_fasta(paste0(efetch,
  "id=NC_003070.9&seq_start=25048158&seq_stop=25049667&strand=2&rettype=fasta"))
mrna    <- read_fasta(paste0(efetch, "id=NM_105379.4&rettype=fasta"))

# exon 1 = 589 nt, intron 1 = 106 nt, exon 2 = 135 nt, intron 2 = 136 nt, exon 3 = 544 nt
intron_start <- c(589 + 1, 589 + 106 + 135 + 1)
intron_end   <- intron_start + c(106, 136) - 1
introns <- substring(genomic, intron_start, intron_end)
substr(introns, 1, 2)                                   # first two bases
substring(introns, nchar(introns) - 1, nchar(introns))  # last two bases

exons <- substring(genomic, c(1, 696, 967), c(589, 830, 1510))
identical(paste(exons, collapse = ""), mrna)            # splicing in silico

gc <- function(s) round(100 * mean(strsplit(s, "")[[1]] %in% c("G", "C")), 1)
sapply(introns, gc, USE.NAMES = FALSE)
gc(paste(exons, collapse = ""))

(589 - 418) / 3      # codons encoded by exon 1 (418 = 5' UTR length from B2)
```

a. Which two bases start and which two end each intron?
b. Is the spliced genomic sequence identical to the mRNA?
c. What is the GC content (%) of the two introns and of the exons together?
d. How many codons of the CDS lie in exon 1? UniProt annotates residues 1–54 of
   P10795 as the chloroplast **transit peptide**. Which exon encodes it?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

```
[1] "GT" "GT"
[1] "AG" "AG"
[1] TRUE
[1] 23.6 24.3
[1] 42.7
[1] 57
```

a. Both introns start with **GT** and end with **AG**, the GT–AG rule that the
   spliceosome recognises.
b. **Yes** (`TRUE`): removing the introns gives exactly the mRNA.
c. Introns **23.6 %** and **24.3 %**, exons **42.7 %**. Plant introns are
   typically AT-rich, which helps the splicing machinery find them.
d. **57** codons, so the whole **transit peptide (54 aa) is encoded by exon 1**.
   The address that sends the small subunit into the chloroplast is a separate
   module of the gene; the mature enzyme part is mostly encoded by exons 2
   and 3.
:::

### B4. The other half of Rubisco is made in the chloroplast

a. Search NCBI Gene for `rbcL[sym] AND "Arabidopsis thaliana"[orgn]`. On which
   genome is the gene, and what are its coordinates? Then search Ensembl
   Plants for **ATCG00490**: how many exons does rbcL have?

The code fetches the rbcL gene from the chloroplast genome (NC_000932.1) and
both proteins from UniProt (O03042 large subunit, P10795 small subunit).

```r
efetch <- "https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/efetch.fcgi?db=nuccore&"
read_fasta <- function(url) paste(readLines(url)[-1], collapse = "")
rbcL  <- read_fasta(paste0(efetch,
  "id=NC_000932.1&seq_start=54958&seq_stop=56397&strand=1&rettype=fasta"))
large <- read_fasta("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/O03042.fasta")
small <- read_fasta("https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P10795.fasta")

c(rbcL_nt = nchar(rbcL), large_aa = nchar(large))
nchar(rbcL) / 3 - 1
substr(rbcL, 1, 3); substr(rbcL, nchar(rbcL) - 2, nchar(rbcL))
substr(large, 1, 10)
substr(small, 1, 10)

c(large = nchar(large), mature_small = nchar(small) - 54)
```

b. Is the rbcL gene a single uninterrupted CDS? Check: does its length fit
   3 × (protein length + 1), and what are its first and last codons?
c. Does the large subunit need a chloroplast transit peptide? (Look at its
   first residues and at the Features of O03042.)
d. The small subunit loses its 54-residue transit peptide in the chloroplast;
   count the large subunit as 479 aa. UniProt says the enzyme is a
   "heterohexadecamer of 8 large chains and 8 small chains". How many amino
   acids are in one Rubisco holoenzyme, and what fraction of them is encoded by
   the nucleus?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. The **chloroplast** genome (NC_000932.1), nucleotides **54958–56397**
   (Gene ID 844754; the chloroplast genome is about 154 kb, chromosome 1 about
   30 Mb). Ensembl shows **one** exon, on region "Pt", forward strand.

```
 rbcL_nt large_aa
    1440      479
[1] 479
[1] "ATG"
[1] "TAG"
[1] "MSPQTETKAS"
[1] "MASSMLSSAT"
       large mature_small
         479          126
```

b. **Yes**: 1440 = 3 × (479 + 1), starting with **ATG** and ending with the
   stop codon **TAG**, with no introns.
c. **No.** It is made by chloroplast ribosomes where it works. UniProt only
   annotates a 2-residue propeptide (1–2), not a transit peptide; the
   nuclear-encoded small subunit starts with the transit peptide MASSML….
d. Large **479**, mature small **126** (180 − 54). One holoenzyme has
   8 × 479 + 8 × 126 = **4840** amino acids, of which 1008/4840 ≈ **21 %** come
   from nuclear genes (removing the large subunit's 2-residue propeptide
   hardly changes this). Building Rubisco needs the two genomes to be expressed
   in step.
:::

### B5. A plant without root hairs

Root hairs enlarge the absorbing surface of a root. Mutants in the gene
**ROOT HAIR DEFECTIVE 6 (RHD6)** make almost no root hairs.

a. Search NCBI Gene for `RHD6[sym] AND "Arabidopsis thaliana"[orgn]` (or TAIR
   for "RHD6"). What is its AGI code? Is it on the same chromosome as RBCS1A,
   and which of the two genes lies closer to the top of the chromosome?
b. Open the gene in Ensembl Plants. How many exons does transcript
   AT1G66470.1 have, and on which strand is the gene?
c. In UniProt (entry Q9C707), what type of protein is RHD6, where is it in the
   cell, and which residues form its domain?

Ensembl gives the exon lengths 640, 105, 66, 66 and 549 nt for AT1G66470.1,
and the CDS starts at nucleotide 113 of the mRNA. The gene spans 1802 bp. The
code finds which exon encodes a given amino acid.

```r
exon_len <- c(640, 105, 66, 66, 549)    # AT1G66470.1, exons in transcript order
utr5     <- 112                         # CDS starts at nucleotide 113 of the mRNA
sum(exon_len)                           # mRNA length
1802 - sum(exon_len)                    # total intron length (gene = 1802 bp)

exon_end <- cumsum(exon_len)            # last mRNA nucleotide of each exon
codon_exon <- function(aa) {            # which exon holds the first base of codon aa?
  nt <- utr5 + 3 * (aa - 1) + 1
  which(nt <= exon_end)[1]
}
codon_exon(1)
codon_exon(201)                         # start of the bHLH domain
codon_exon(250)                         # end of the bHLH domain
codon_exon(298)
```

d. What are the mRNA length and the total intron length?
e. Which exons encode the bHLH domain?
f. Check the CDS: the protein has 298 aa. How long must the CDS be?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. **AT1G66470**, Gene ID 842965. Same chromosome (**1**); its number 66470
   is lower than 67090, so **RHD6** lies closer to the top. The two genes are
   about 250 kb apart (RHD6 ends at 24797015, RBCS1A starts at 25048158), with
   roughly 60 gene numbers between them.
b. **5** exons, **forward** strand (RBCS1A was on the reverse strand:
   neighbouring genes can be read from opposite strands).
c. A **transcription factor** of the **bHLH** (basic helix-loop-helix) family,
   located in the **nucleus**; bHLH domain = residues **201–250**.

```
[1] 1426
[1] 376
[1] 1
[1] 2
[1] 4
[1] 5
```

d. mRNA **1426** nt; introns **376** nt in total (4 introns).
e. **Exons 2 to 4** (codon 201 is in exon 2, codon 250 in exon 4). The
   DNA-binding domain is split across three exons.
f. 3 × (298 + 1) = **897** nt. A transcription factor in the nucleus that
   switches on root-hair genes in some epidermal cells: a change in one gene's
   expression alters the absorbing surface of the whole root system.
:::
